主要内容: Zambia's spiraling debt and the future of Chinese loan financing in Africa have become a focal point of global financial discussions. China has provided billions of dollars in loans for infrastructure projects across Sub-Saharan Africa, with Zambia being one of the most prominent debtors. Recent research from EXX Africa indicates that Chinese firms are seeking control of Zambian mining assets as collateral for potential loan defaults. Zambia is currently restructuring, renegotiating, or refinancing its extensive Chinese project finance debt, but Chinese companies are showing little patience and are instead seeking fresh collateral in case of default. The country's sovereign debt is expected to reach 96% of GDP in 2020, and it has defaulted on a spree of loans in 2019, including a $107 million loan from Italian bank Intesa Sanpaolo. The International Monetary Fund has withheld credit facilities due to concerns over Zambia's high debt and shrinking foreign exchange reserves. Zambian GDP has halved to just 2% over the past three years, and the kwacha currency has depreciated by almost 17% against the dollar. President Edgar Lungu has stated that his government will seek to reduce domestic arrears and maintain debt within sustainable levels. Chinese financial institutions are increasingly seeking control over Zambian mining assets as collateral for loans. Chinese companies, including China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation, are reportedly seeking restructuring of loan agreements that could involve mining assets being placed as collateral. Negotiations are likely being conducted by China Exim Bank, Sinosure (China Export & Credit Corporation), and Chinese government officials. Additionally, China retains a highly contentious stake in Zambia's national broadcaster, ZNBC. In 2017, Chinese media conglomerate StarTimes funded the rollout of a migration to a new digital TV signal and now controls 60% of a joint digital venture with ZNBC, called TopStar. The venture was also bankrolled by a $232 million loan from Exim Bank and has been criticized by media watchdogs for allegedly granting excessive influence over the media landscape to Beijing. Zambian government representatives did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Sinosure, Exim Bank, and China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation have also been contacted for comment.
